analysis.one_liner: Caps U.S. global warming pollution and requires cleaner cars, power plants, and more renewable electricity.
analysis.headline: The first comprehensive Senate bill to cut U.S. global warming pollution 80% by 2050 was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 109th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have written mandatory limits on carbon dioxide and other heat-trapping gases into the Clean Air Act for the first time, requiring U.S. emissions to return to 1990 levels by 2020 and fall 80% below 1990 levels by 2050. It set greenhouse gas standards for new cars starting in model year 2016 and for power plants, required electricity suppliers to meet a renewable energy standard reaching 20% by 2020 and yearly efficiency savings targets, mandated a low-carbon generation credit program for coal-based generators, and directed the Securities and Exchange Commission to make companies disclose climate-related financial risks to investors. The EPA could run the cuts through a market-based cap-and-trade program with cost controls, and allowances could fund transition help for households, communities, and workers hit hardest by the shift to a low-carbon economy.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people, through reduced exposure to climate-driven disasters, cleaner air from reduced fossil fuel combustion, lower electricity use from the efficiency targets, and better information as investors gain mandatory climate-risk disclosures. The renewable energy, biofuel, and energy-efficiency industries would also gain large new markets: a national renewable electricity standard reaching 20% of sales by 2020, credits for low-carbon generation, and a 5-billion-gallon annual low-carbon renewable fuel requirement from 2015.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Households, renewable energy, and efficiency industries

how_it_helps.text: The bill directs EPA to cut aggregate U.S. global warming pollution to 1990 levels by 2020 and 80% below 1990 levels by 2050, with the stated goal of keeping global warming under 2 degrees Celsius.

Every manufacturer's car fleet must meet greenhouse gas emission standards beginning with model year 2016, and new power plants must emit no more than a new combined-cycle natural gas unit, with all units subject to the standard by 2030.

Retail electricity suppliers must cut customer electricity use and peak demand on an escalating annual schedule (reaching 9% cumulative electricity savings and 11.75% peak-demand reduction from 2020 onward) and meet a renewable electricity requirement of 20% of sales by 2020, with credits tradeable and fees for suppliers that miss the targets.

Emission allowances not given to covered polluters may be allocated to households, communities, and companies suffering disproportionate harm from the transition, plus owners of efficient buildings, sequestration projects, and ecosystem restoration efforts.

The bill requires the SEC to force securities issuers to disclose their global warming pollution exposure and climate risks to investors, and requires federal environmental reviews to consider global warming effects.

analysis.who_pays: Coal-burning electric utilities, oil refiners, and automakers would bear the direct compliance costs: power plants face emission standards and low-carbon generation mandates, gasoline must include low-carbon renewable fuel, and vehicle fleets must meet emission caps. Some of those costs would likely be passed on to consumers through higher electricity, gasoline, and vehicle prices, though the bill's allowance allocations and efficiency savings are designed to offset some of this.
analysis.who_pays_short: Coal utilities, oil refiners, and automakers

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs for power plants and refiners would be partly passed through to consumers in the form of higher electricity, heating, and gasoline prices, especially in the transition years before 2020.

The bill builds in cost relief: the cap can pause at a 'technology-indexed stop price' when the allowance price exceeds the cost of deploying clean technologies, and standards can be delayed if the National Academy of Sciences finds them technologically infeasible — flexibility that a critic could call loopholes that weaken the emission cuts.

The 5-billion-gallon annual low-carbon renewable fuel mandate channels money into the biofuel industry, and requiring renewable fuel in gasoline raises food-versus-fuel and land-use concerns an honest supporter would have to acknowledge.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is an aggressive but technically careful design: it pairs the deepest emission cuts ever proposed in the Senate at the time with cost controls, safety valves, and transition assistance for hard-hit households and workers. The main honest tradeoff is short-term energy price pressure on consumers versus long-term avoidance of climate damage, with the pass-through of industry compliance costs the principal cost. The bill was never debated on the merits, so its design was never tested in negotiation.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on July 20, 2006, read twice, and referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, where it sat without a hearing, markup, or floor vote until the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.

narrative.text: Senator James Jeffords, the chamber's only Independent, introduced the bill on July 20, 2006, joined in the introduction by nine Democratic colleagues including Barbara Boxer, Edward Kennedy, and Patrick Leahy.
The bill drew 11 cosponsors, all of them Senate Democrats.
After its introduction, the only action ever taken was that the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Environment and Public Works.
The full action history shows no hearing, no committee markup, no committee report, and no floor vote at any point before the 109th Congress expired on January 3, 2007.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coal-fired electric utilities, oil companies, and automakers that would have faced mandatory emission limits, along with the Senate majority that avoided a vote on them, were better off because the bill died. They kept operating under no federal carbon limits for another Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Coal utilities, oil companies, and automakers

sides.party_line_note: Every cosponsor was a Senate Democrat (11 of 44) behind the chamber's only Independent sponsor; no Republican signed on, and the bill died in the Republican-controlled committee without a hearing or vote.

industries.industry: Coal-fired electric utilities and coal mining
industries.note: New plants would have to match the emission rate of a new natural gas combined-cycle unit and existing units by 2030, and coal-based generators would owe escalating low-carbon generation percentages. But the bill also builds a compliance path and subsidy structure for coal — geological disposal grants, sequestration credit rules, and a credit-trading program — so it would have regulated coal while entrenching it as the pay-to-clean channel.

Each manufacturer's fleet would have had to meet greenhouse gas emission caps beginning with model year 2016, roughly in line with California-style standards. Compliance costs would fall on the companies and partly on car buyers.

Gasoline would have been required to contain 5 billion gallons of low-carbon renewable fuel annually from 2015 onward, a costly mandate for refiners. The consumer gain is lower emissions rather than lower prices.

A national renewable electricity standard reaching 20% of sales by 2020, escalating utility efficiency targets with tradeable credits, and low-carbon generation credits would have created guaranteed demand. This gain runs directly alongside the public interest in cheaper, cleaner electricity.

The low-carbon renewable fuel mandate and Agriculture Department accreditation of biological carbon sequestration would have opened revenue streams for fuel producers and landowners, though the 75% emissions-reduction bar means corn ethanol may not have qualified.
